title: Plaques and Patients
passage:
In February 2022 a hospital sent Rhiannon Bellinghast’s laboratory a request it could not fill. The patient was a man in his sixties whose knee replacement had been infected for eleven months, through two washouts and four antibiotics, and his surgeons wanted to know whether anything in the laboratory’s freezers would kill the strain he was carrying. Technicians spread his isolate over ninety plates, dropped a different phage onto each one, and waited. A phage is a virus that infects bacteria and nothing else; where it takes hold, the bacteria die in a widening circle and leave a clear spot – a plaque – in the film of growth. Ninety plates came back cloudy. The knee came out in April. Cases that end that way rarely reach print, which is worth saying before any of the numbers that follow.

What Bellinghast’s group has and most hospitals do not is the collection itself: 1,140 phages gathered since 2016 from sewage outfalls, hospital drains and, in one productive week, a duck pond, of which some four hundred have been sequenced and described in full. Each phage fastens onto a particular molecule on the bacterial surface, so a phage that clears one patient’s strain may do nothing whatever to the strain in the next room. There is no broad-spectrum version to fall back on. Over five years the collection has produced a usable match for rather more than half of the isolates sent to it, and that figure hides a spread: close to three in four for Klebsiella, well under half for the staphylococci that dominate infected implants. Bellinghast says the gap has not narrowed as the collection has grown, which is not what she expected when she began adding to it.

The clinical record is thin, and honest about being thin. A series published last year followed sixty-three patients treated at four hospitals between 2020 and 2024; in forty-one the infection was under control at six months, and eleven had the implant taken out anyway. Every patient in it was also on antibiotics, since withholding them would have been indefensible, and the hospitals had referred the cases they judged most likely to respond. “Our results suggest that phages add something in a subset of these infections,” Bellinghast says. “They cannot tell us how large that something is.” She is careful about what the series will bear, and the care is warranted: without a comparison group, a recovery in a patient taking four drugs says little about the fifth. Josephine Quilvey, who treats bone and joint infection at one of the four hospitals, is readier than that. She would offer a matched phage as a standard option in infected joint replacements, where the alternative is often a second operation to take the implant out, and she is deliberate about the limit: she means that setting, not resistant infection at large.

Bacteria adapt to phages much as they adapt to drugs, usually by altering the very molecule the phage has to grip, and the field has a hopeful story about what that alteration costs them. The molecule is often one the bacterium needs as well, so an escape mutant ought to hold less firmly to an implant, or to become vulnerable again to an antibiotic it had shrugged off. Bellinghast’s group sequenced thirty-four escape mutants recovered from patients during treatment. Nine had paid a price of that kind. The other twenty-five clung to plastic and grew as strongly as the strains they came from. Putting several phages into a single preparation makes escape less likely without abolishing it, and every such mixture is made for one named patient, which is where the paperwork starts.

The part of all this that has genuinely improved is unglamorous. In 2021 the median time between a hospital sending an isolate and a preparation coming back was nineteen days, which is longer than most of these decisions can wait; last year it was six, on the strength of a courier contract, a technician on call over the weekend, and a decision to stop fully sequencing a phage before it is used. A randomized trial in prosthetic joint infection is now enrolling at two of the four hospitals, and that trial, not any series, will decide whether the treatment becomes ordinary. The isolate from February 2022 is still in a freezer two floors below the plate room. Two hundred phages have joined the collection since; none of them clears it.
– Neil Hollowmere, science correspondent

isolate = a bacterial sample grown from one patient and kept as a pure culture
plaque = the clear spot left on a plate where phages have killed the bacteria growing there

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: Why joint implants become infected so often, and what surgeons do when the treatment fails.
How sewage and hospital drains have become the leading source of new medicines.
How phages are matched to particular infections, and how far the results so far reach.
Why resistant bacteria are spreading faster than new antibiotics can be brought to market.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text focus), edge position 1. WHY-KEY (C): the passage runs matching first and evidence second – the failed screen of ninety plates, the collection and its species-dependent match rate, the sixty-three-patient series and what it cannot support, the escape mutants, and the trial that will decide the question. C names both strands, the procedure and the reach of the findings, without asserting a verdict the text withholds. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = scope_error – it promotes the opening case and the removed knee, the passage's most vivid material, to the subject of the whole text; the text never explains why implants become infected and mentions surgery only as the alternative that phage treatment might displace. B = surface_word_match – it recycles the distinctive sourcing detail ("sewage outfalls, hospital drains") into a claim about medicine at large that the passage never makes; the drains supply this one collection, not a leading source of new medicines. D = outside_knowledge – a true-sounding statement about resistance and the antibiotic pipeline that the passage never argues; it is tempting because resistant infection is the setting of every case described, but the text's argument is about matching and evidence, not about the pace of drug development.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the collection of phages that Bellinghast’s group keeps?

options.text: Staphylococci are matched more readily than Klebsiella, which is why implant infections respond well.
Every strain sent to the laboratory has been matched to a phage sooner or later.
About four hundred of its phages have so far been given to patients.
Rather more than half of the samples it is sent find a usable match.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), local order, anchored in paragraph 2. WHY-KEY (D): the passage states that over five years the collection "has produced a usable match for rather more than half of the isolates sent to it". D paraphrases that figure in different words and claims no more than the sentence does. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = swapped particulars plus a causal graft – the passage gives Klebsiella the higher rate ("close to three in four") and the staphylococci the lower one ("well under half"), so A inverts the two named rates, and it then glues on a consequence about implant infections responding well that the passage nowhere states; tempting because both organisms and both figures come from the same sentence. B = quantifier_upgrade – it takes the real matching procedure and absolutizes it into universal success, which the opening paragraph refutes directly, since ninety plates came back cloudy and that patient never got a phage. C = surface_word_match with a swapped referent – the figure of about four hundred is real but counts the phages that "have been sequenced and described in full", not phages given to patients; the passage never says how many of the collection have been used clinically, and the one series it reports covers sixty-three patients in all. Tempting because the number is quoted accurately from the paragraph the stem points at.

questions.prompt: What does the text say about the sixty-three patients in the published series?

options.text: In about two thirds the infection was under control at six months, alongside antibiotics.
All of them kept the implant once the phage preparation had been given.
The most difficult cases were referred first, and it was those patients who did best.
Their outcomes were compared with those of patients given antibiotics alone.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), local order, anchored in paragraph 3. WHY-KEY (A): the passage reports that of sixty-three patients "in forty-one the infection was under control at six months", which is about two thirds, and that "Every patient in it was also on antibiotics". A carries both facts and nothing else. WHY-DISTRACTORS: B = quantifier_upgrade – it converts the partial result into a clean sweep and ignores the eleven patients who "had the implant taken out anyway"; tempting to a reader who registers the forty-one and stops. C = inverted attribution of the referral pattern – the hospitals "had referred the cases they judged most likely to respond", which is the opposite of sending the most difficult ones, and the passage says nothing at all about which patients within the series fared best; tempting because selection is discussed in that very sentence. D = outside_knowledge about method – it supplies the controlled comparison a reader expects a published series to contain, while the passage says the opposite in the next sentence ("without a comparison group"); tempting because the trial mentioned in the last paragraph does promise exactly this design, later and elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What is implied about the hope that escaping a phage leaves a bacterium weaker?

options.text: It is confirmed: escape always costs the bacterium something.
It will probably be settled by the trial now enrolling at two hospitals.
It holds for a minority of escape mutants, not as a rule.
It is groundless, since none of the mutants turned out to be weakened at all.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 4. WHY-KEY (C): the passage sets out the hopeful story (the molecule the phage grips is often one the bacterium needs, so an escape mutant "ought to" hold less firmly or turn vulnerable again), then reports the numbers that test it: nine of thirty-four escape mutants "had paid a price of that kind", while "the other twenty-five clung to plastic and grew as strongly as the strains they came from". The implication is that the trade-off is real in a minority and cannot be relied on, which is what C says. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = quantifier_upgrade – it hardens a nine-in-thirty-four finding into a law with "always"; tempting because the passage does describe the mechanism that would make the cost general. B = wrong_location, hedged in form so that qualification alone does not identify the key – the trial in the final paragraph is enrolling to decide whether the treatment becomes routine, not to test what escape costs a bacterium. D = polarity overshoot in the other direction – it discards the hope entirely, which the nine mutants that did pay a price directly refute; tempting to a reader who reads the twenty-five as the whole result.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude toward putting phage treatment into routine use?

options.text: Dismissive, treating the whole approach as a distraction from proper antibiotic care.
Interested, but unwilling to let the results so far settle the question.
Persuaded, with Quilvey, that matched phages should already be a standard option.
Detached, reporting the case for and against without any view of his own.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / tone / attitude), edge position 5, signature trap role_or_attribution_swap. WHY-KEY (B): the writer's own judgments are placed sparingly and all point the same way – he opens on a failure and remarks that such cases "rarely reach print, which is worth saying before any of the numbers that follow"; he endorses Bellinghast's hedge outright ("the care is warranted") and explains why ("without a comparison group, a recovery in a patient taking four drugs says little about the fifth"); and he states that the enrolling trial, "not any series, will decide whether the treatment becomes ordinary". He devotes the whole passage to the work, so he is plainly interested; he refuses to let any of the reported results decide the question. WHY-DISTRACTORS: C = role_or_attribution_swap – Quilvey's readiness to use a matched phage as a standard option is her position, offered in her own voice and immediately fenced by her own limit; the writer reports it without joining it. A = polarity overshoot – nothing in the passage treats the approach as a distraction, and the closing paragraph credits a real improvement in the pipeline. D = tone_misread – the writer is restrained but not view-free, and the three evaluative markers above (worth saying, the care is warranted, that trial will decide) are exactly the sentences a detached reporter would not write.
